text: NASA finds no Apophis impact risk for at least the next 100 years
as_written: no impact risk from it for at least the next hundred years
source: NASA/JPL Center for Near Earth Object Studies (CNEOS) and NASA statement following March 2021 radar observations

text: Impacts in 2029, 2036 and 2068 have been ruled out
as_written: it will not hit us in twenty twenty-nine, or in twenty thirty-six, or in twenty sixty-eight
source: NASA/JPL CNEOS; Goldstone and Green Bank radar observations, March 2021

text: Apophis is about 340 metres across
as_written: about three hundred and forty metres across
source: Brozovic et al. 2018, Icarus, radar shape model of 99942 Apophis

text: The Eiffel Tower is roughly 330 metres tall
as_written: roughly as wide as the Eiffel Tower is tall
source: Eiffel Tower operator (SETE) published height

text: Apophis mass is about 60 million tonnes
as_written: around sixty million tonnes
source: Brozovic et al. 2018, Icarus (about 6 x 10^10 kg)

text: Impact speed would be about 12 km/s
as_written: about twelve kilometres every second
source: Derived from JPL Small-Body Database orbit of Apophis combined with Earth escape velocity of 11.2 km/s

text: 12 km/s is more than thirty times the speed of sound
as_written: more than thirty times the speed of sound
source: Derived: 12 km/s divided by 0.343 km/s

text: Kinetic energy is about 1,200 megatons of TNT
as_written: near twelve hundred megatons of TNT
source: Derived from half mass times speed squared using Brozovic et al. 2018 mass; 1 megaton = 4.184 x 10^15 J

text: Tsar Bomba, tested 1961, yielded about 50 megatons
as_written: the Soviet Tsar Bomba in nineteen sixty-one, was about fifty megatons
source: Historical record of the 30 October 1961 test; widely cited yield of 50 Mt

text: Apophis energy is about 24 Tsar Bombas
as_written: roughly twenty-four of those
source: Derived: 1,200 Mt divided by 50 Mt

text: Apophis energy is about 80,000 Hiroshima bombs
as_written: something like eighty thousand Hiroshima bombs
source: Derived: 1,200 Mt divided by about 15 kt Hiroshima yield (US government estimates)

text: Energy is delivered in a fraction of a second
as_written: in a fraction of a second
source: Derived: 340 m body stopping at about 12 km/s takes under 0.1 s

text: Apophis was discovered in June 2004 at Kitt Peak, Arizona
as_written: June of two thousand four. Astronomers at Kitt Peak in Arizona
source: Minor Planet Center discovery record (Tucker, Tholen, Bernardi, 19 June 2004)

text: Apophis is named for the Egyptian serpent of chaos
as_written: after the Egyptian serpent of chaos
source: IAU/Minor Planet Center naming of 99942 Apophis; NASA/JPL

text: In December 2004 the 2029 impact odds peaked near 1 in 37, about 2.7 percent
as_written: climb to about one in thirty-seven
source: NASA/JPL CNEOS Apophis history; NASA Planetary Defense statements

text: Apophis reached 4 on the Torino scale, the highest rating any object has received
as_written: the highest rating any object has ever received
source: NASA/JPL CNEOS Torino Scale record

text: Torino 4 means a close encounter with at least a 1 percent chance of a collision capable of regional devastation
as_written: at least a one percent chance of a collision capable of regional devastation
source: Torino Impact Hazard Scale definition (IAU/NASA)

text: Archived March 2004 images removed the 2029 risk on 27 December 2004
as_written: On the twenty-seventh of December, astronomers find older photographs of the same dot, taken in March of that year
source: NASA/JPL CNEOS; precovery images from Siding Spring Observatory

text: 13 April 2029 is a Friday
as_written: is a Friday
source: Gregorian calendar

text: Closest approach is about 32,000 km from Earth's centre
as_written: about thirty-two thousand kilometres from the centre of the Earth
source: NASA/JPL CNEOS close-approach data for 99942 Apophis

text: That is inside the geostationary ring, which is about 42,164 km from Earth's centre
as_written: inside the ring of geostationary satellites
source: Standard geostationary orbit radius, about 42,164 km

text: Distance is about one twelfth of the Moon's distance
as_written: about one twelfth of the way to the Moon
source: Derived: mean Earth-Moon distance 384,400 km divided by about 32,000 km

text: Apophis will be visible to the naked eye from Europe, Africa and western Asia
as_written: People across Europe, Africa and western Asia will be able to see it without a telescope
source: NASA and ESA descriptions of the 2029 flyby

text: A gravitational keyhole a few hundred metres wide would have set up a 2036 return
as_written: a patch of space called a gravitational keyhole, only a few hundred metres wide
source: Chesley 2005, IAU Symposium 229 (keyhole about 600 m wide); NASA/JPL

text: Radar in March 2021 cleared 2068
as_written: Radar measurements in March of twenty twenty-one then cleared twenty sixty-eight as well
source: NASA/JPL news release, March 2021, Goldstone and Green Bank radar

text: Apophis's orbit period is just under a year before the flyby and longer than a year after
as_written: Before the flyby, Apophis circles the Sun in a little under a year. After it, Earth's gravity will have stretched its orbit to something longer than a year
source: NASA/JPL CNEOS orbit solution; Apophis moves from Aten-class to Apollo-class orbit

text: The edge of space is conventionally 100 km
as_written: a hundred kilometres of altitude, the line most people call the edge of space
source: Karman line, Federation Aeronautique Internationale

text: About eight seconds to cross 100 km at about 12 km/s
as_written: about eight seconds of atmosphere ahead of it
source: Derived: 100 km divided by about 12.6 km/s

text: About ten tonnes of air sit above each square metre
as_written: about ten tonnes of air
source: Standard atmosphere, 101,325 Pa divided by g

text: Air in a column as wide as Apophis weighs about one sixtieth of the rock
as_written: about one sixtieth as much as the rock
source: Derived: cross-section about 91,000 square metres times about 10 t/m2, versus 6 x 10^7 t

text: Chelyabinsk 2013: about 20 m object, about 500 kt, over a thousand injured
as_written: a stone about twenty metres wide burst high above Chelyabinsk in Russia with the energy of roughly five hundred kilotons, and the blast broke enough windows to injure more than a thousand people
source: Popova et al. 2013, Science; Russian emergency ministry casualty reports

text: Tunguska 1908: roughly 50-60 m object flattened about 2,000 square km of forest
as_written: perhaps fifty or sixty metres wide flattened about two thousand square kilometres of Siberian forest
source: Chyba, Thomas and Zahnle 1993, Nature; Boslough and Crawford 2008; Russian forest-fall surveys

text: Tunguska energy estimates range from about 3 to 30 megatons
as_written: estimates running from about three to thirty megatons
source: Boslough and Crawford 2008; Longo 2007 review of Tunguska

text: Shock-heated air at hypervelocity exceeds the Sun's surface temperature
as_written: hotter than the surface of the sun
source: Melosh 1989, Impact Cratering: A Geologic Process

text: The whole asteroid is stopped in under a tenth of a second
as_written: under a tenth of a second for the whole asteroid to be stopped
source: Derived: 340 m divided by about 12 km/s is about 0.03 s, longer at an oblique angle

text: Peak shock pressure is millions of times atmospheric
as_written: the pressure is millions of times that of the atmosphere
source: Melosh 1989, Impact Cratering; planar impact approximation

text: Transient cavity about 4 km wide, final crater 4 to 5 km
as_written: a temporary cavity about four kilometres wide and more than a kilometre deep
source: Collins, Melosh and Marcus 2005, Earth Impact Effects Program scaling

text: Most likely impact angle is 45 degrees
as_written: At the most likely impact angle, forty-five degrees
source: Gilbert 1893; Shoemaker 1962

text: Meteor Crater is about 1.2 km wide, formed about 50,000 years ago by an object roughly 50 m across
as_written: about one point two kilometres wide, and it was dug about fifty thousand years ago by an iron meteorite only around fifty metres across
source: Melosh and Collins 2005, Nature; USGS and Meteoritical Society

text: Speed of sound is about 340 m/s
as_written: about three hundred and forty metres per second
source: Standard value at sea level

text: Blast arrives almost five minutes after the flash at 100 km
as_written: it arrives almost five minutes after the flash
source: Derived: 100,000 m divided by 343 m/s is about 290 s

text: Seismic waves travel at several km/s
as_written: Shaking travels through rock at several kilometres per second
source: USGS seismic wave velocities

text: Blast can break windows beyond 100 km
as_written: shatter windows more than a hundred kilometres from the crater
source: Collins et al. 2005 Earth Impact Effects Program; nuclear-effects overpressure scaling (rough estimate)

text: Oceans cover about 71 percent of Earth
as_written: About seventy-one percent of Earth's surface is ocean
source: NOAA

text: Average ocean depth is about 3.7 km
as_written: The average depth is roughly three point seven kilometres
source: NOAA ocean facts

text: Ward and Asphaug 2000 modelled asteroid impact tsunami hazard
as_written: Early work in the year two thousand, by Steven Ward and Erik Asphaug
source: Ward and Asphaug 2000, Icarus 145, Asteroid impact tsunami

text: Later simulations found impact waves lose energy quickly
as_written: Later computer simulations, including work at Los Alamos National Laboratory
source: Gisler, Weaver and Gittings 2011, Computing in Science and Engineering; Melosh, impact tsunami reviews

text: About 1 km is the commonly cited threshold for global effects
as_written: an asteroid about one kilometre wide as the rough threshold for global damage
source: NASA Planetary Defense Coordination Office; Toon et al. 1997, Reviews of Geophysics

text: Apophis has about 25 times less mass than a 1 km body
as_written: it carries about twenty-five times less mass
source: Derived: (1000/340) cubed is about 25

text: Pinatubo 1991 cooled the planet by about 0.5 C for a year or two
as_written: cooled the planet by about half a degree Celsius for a year or two
source: USGS and NASA Earth Observatory

text: Tambora 1815 was followed by the year without a summer in 1816
as_written: the eruption of Tambora in eighteen fifteen was followed by the year without a summer
source: Standard volcanology and climate history, e.g. Oppenheimer 2003

text: Chicxulub impactor about 10 km wide, about 66 million years ago, energy tens of thousands of times Apophis
as_written: It was around ten kilometres wide, and its energy was tens of thousands of times greater than Apophis's
source: Schulte et al. 2010, Science; Collins et al. 2020; energy ratio derived

text: Objects of this size strike about once every tens of thousands of years
as_written: only about once every tens of thousands of years
source: NASA Planetary Defense Coordination Office; NEO Science Definition Team 2017

text: Solar power intercepted by Earth is about 1.7 x 10^17 W
as_written: about one hundred and seventy quadrillion watts
source: Kopp and Lean 2011 total solar irradiance; NASA

text: Apophis energy equals about 28 seconds of sunlight on Earth
as_written: you get about twenty-eight seconds
source: Derived: about 4.8 x 10^18 J divided by 1.74 x 10^17 W

text: Earth orbits the Sun at nearly 30 km/s
as_written: nearly thirty kilometres every second
source: NASA Earth Fact Sheet (29.78 km/s)

text: About 1,800 km per minute
as_written: about eighteen hundred kilometres each minute
source: Derived: 29.8 km/s times 60

text: Effective target with gravitational focusing is about 27,000 km wide
as_written: our effective target is roughly twenty-seven thousand kilometres wide
source: Derived from Earth radius 6,371 km and gravitational focusing factor of about 4.6 for 12.6 km/s impact and 11.2 km/s escape speed

text: A few minutes to a quarter hour timing shift suffices to miss
as_written: somewhere between a few minutes and a quarter of an hour early or late
source: Derived: 27,000 km divided by 1,800 km/min is about 15 min for the full width

text: A deflection of about 1 to 2 cm/s a decade ahead suffices
as_written: a change in the asteroid's speed of about a centimetre or two per second would do it
source: Derived from along-track drift of about 3 times delta-v times time; see NASA NEO Survey and Deflection Study

text: That is less than one part in a million of Apophis's orbital speed
as_written: That is less than one part in a million
source: Derived: 0.02 m/s divided by about 30,000 m/s; orbit from JPL Small-Body Database

text: DART mass about 570 kg, speed about 6 km/s, target Dimorphos about 160 m wide
as_written: about five hundred and seventy kilograms, flew into Dimorphos, a moonlet roughly one hundred and sixty metres wide, at about six kilometres per second
source: NASA DART mission; Daly et al. 2023, Nature

text: Dimorphos orbit shortened from 11 h 55 min to about 11 h 23 min, a 32 minute change
as_written: from eleven hours and fifty-five minutes to about eleven hours and twenty-three minutes, a change of thirty-two minutes
source: Thomas et al. 2023, Nature; NASA DART results

text: Speed change was a few mm/s and ejecta enhanced the push roughly 3 to 4 times
as_written: The speed change was only a few millimetres per second, and the debris thrown off gave an extra shove, roughly three to four times larger
source: Cheng et al. 2023, Nature (momentum enhancement factor about 3.6)

text: Apophis is about 14 times as massive as Dimorphos
as_written: Apophis is about fourteen times more massive than Dimorphos
source: Brozovic et al. 2018 (Apophis) and Daly et al. 2023 (Dimorphos about 4.3 x 10^9 kg); ratio derived

text: About a hundred DART-class impacts would be needed
as_written: on the order of a hundred such impacts
source: Derived back-of-envelope momentum comparison using DART beta of about 3.6

text: Apophis tumbles with a period of about 30.5 hours
as_written: about thirty and a half hours to complete one cycle
source: Pravec et al. 2014, Icarus (30.56 h)

text: Researchers disagree on whether the 2029 flyby will change the spin or trigger landslides
as_written: some researchers expect our gravity to alter that tumble and even shake loose rock from its surface in landslides. Others expect little change
source: Benson et al. 2023, Icarus; Yu et al. 2014 and related Apophis spin studies

text: OSIRIS-APEX arrives at Apophis soon after the 2029 flyby
as_written: NASA's OSIRIS-APEX spacecraft is due to arrive soon after the flyby
source: NASA OSIRIS-APEX mission
